title: About Me
text:
I am a results-oriented Master’s student in Ireland specialising in Business Analytics and AI-driven business solutions. My work sits at the intersection of international trade and advanced analytics — translating complex data into strategic insights that inform real decisions.
My professional perspective is built upon a foundation in International Trade and Business, further enriched by practical experience in high-volume commercial environments. During my time in customer-facing and operational roles, I developed an acute understanding of how supply chain dynamics, pricing fluctuations, and seasonal trends directly influence consumer behaviour. This firsthand observation of market variables served as the catalyst for my transition into advanced analytics.
I am currently refining my technical proficiency in Python, SQL, and Business Intelligence tools to translate complex datasets into actionable business intelligence. My goal is to combine my international business background with rigorous quantitative analysis to help organisations bridge the gap between global strategy and localised operational impact.

title: Fraud Detection: A Statistical Exploration of Consumer Transaction Data
text:
Fraud detection is one of the most pressing challenges facing the banking sector today. Financial institutions must balance the operational cost of reviewing transactions against the financial and reputational cost of missing fraudulent ones. This project was developed as part of the Statistical Models and Methods for Business Analytics module, and applies the statistical techniques covered in class to a real-sized transaction dataset.






NoteWhat this project covers




Descriptive statistics and outlier detection using IQR and Z-scores
Correlation analysis between demographic, financial, and behavioural variables
Exploratory segmentation by age, gender, education, and marital status
Classification modelling with Decision Trees and Random Forest
Honest reflection on model limitations and what the data can — and cannot — tell us

title: Fraud Detection: A Statistical Exploration of Consumer Transaction Data
text:
The Dataset
The dataset consists of 500 transactions and 23 original variables including demographic features (age, gender, education, marital status, region), financial features (personal and family income, credit score, loan amount), and behavioural features (transaction amount, device type, mobile and internet usage). The two key target variables are is_fraud (binary indicator) and fraud_amount (total monetary loss).


Show loading and feature reconstruction
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

df = pd.read_csv('fraud_detect.csv')

# Reconstruct categorical columns from one-hot for readability in EDA
df['gender'] = df['gender_Female'].map({1: 'Female', 0: 'Male'})

def get_first_match(row, prefix):
    for col in df.columns:
        if col.startswith(prefix) and row[col] == 1:
            return col.replace(prefix, '')
    return 'Unknown'

df['education']        = df.apply(lambda r: get_first_match(r, 'education_'), axis=1)
df['marital_status']   = df.apply(lambda r: get_first_match(r, 'marital_status_'), axis=1)
df['Age Group']        = df.apply(lambda r: get_first_match(r, 'Age Group_'), axis=1)
df['transaction_type'] = df.apply(lambda r: get_first_match(r, 'transaction_type_'), axis=1)
df['device_type']      = df.apply(lambda r: get_first_match(r, 'device_type_'), axis=1)

print(f"Records: {len(df)}")
print(f"Columns: {len(df.columns)}")
print(f"\nFraud distribution:")
print(df['is_fraud'].value_counts())


Records: 500
Columns: 55

Fraud distribution:
is_fraud
0    254
1    246
Name: count, dtype: int64


The dataset is well balanced between fraud (246) and non-fraud (254) cases — a favourable starting point for classification, since class imbalance is one of the most common challenges in fraud modelling.

title: Fraud Detection: A Statistical Exploration of Consumer Transaction Data
text:
Outlier Detection
Outliers are particularly relevant in fraud detection, since fraudulent transactions often appear as extreme values in one or more dimensions. I used two complementary approaches: Z-scores and the IQR method.

Z-Score analysis


Show the code
df_fraud = df[df['is_fraud'] == 1].copy()
numeric_cols = ['age', 'personal_income', 'family_income', 'credit_score',
                'loan_amount', 'transaction_amount', 'fraud_amount',
                'account_age_days', 'num_prev_transactions',
                'avg_transaction_value', 'internet_usage_hrs', 'mobile_usage_hrs']

z_scores_max = {}
for col in numeric_cols:
    z = np.abs((df[col] - df[col].mean()) / df[col].std())
    z_scores_max[col] = z.max()

z_df = pd.DataFrame(list(z_scores_max.items()), columns=['Variable', 'Max Z-Score']).sort_values('Max Z-Score', ascending=True)

fig = px.bar(
    z_df,
    x='Max Z-Score', y='Variable',
    orientation='h',
    title='Maximum Absolute Z-Score per Variable',
    color='Max Z-Score',
    color_continuous_scale='Blues',
    template='plotly_white'
)
fig.add_vline(x=3, line_dash='dash', line_color='red',
              annotation_text="Outlier threshold (Z=3)", annotation_position='top')
fig.update_layout(height=480, font_family='Inter, sans-serif', showlegend=False)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 1: Maximum Z-score per numerical variable. Values above 3 indicate a notable outlier.




Four variables contain notable outliers (Z > 3): fraud_amount reaches over 7 standard deviations above the mean, followed by transaction_amount (~6), loan_amount (~4.8), and mobile_usage_hrs (~3.5). This concentration of extremes in the monetary variables confirms the intuition that fraud is a heavy-tailed phenomenon — most cases are small, but a few are very large.


IQR analysis


Show the code
def count_outliers_iqr(df, cols, multiplier=1.5):
    counts = {}
    for col in cols:
        Q1 = df[col].quantile(0.25)
        Q3 = df[col].quantile(0.75)
        IQR = Q3 - Q1
        lower = Q1 - multiplier * IQR
        upper = Q3 + multiplier * IQR
        counts[col] = len(df[(df[col] < lower) | (df[col] > upper)])
    return pd.Series(counts).sort_values(ascending=True)

outliers = count_outliers_iqr(df, numeric_cols)
outliers_df = outliers.reset_index()
outliers_df.columns = ['Variable', 'Outlier Count']

fig = px.bar(
    outliers_df,
    x='Outlier Count', y='Variable',
    orientation='h',
    title='Outliers Detected (1.5 × IQR method)',
    color='Outlier Count',
    color_continuous_scale='Blues',
    template='plotly_white'
)
fig.update_layout(height=480, font_family='Inter, sans-serif', showlegend=False)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 2: Number of outliers detected per variable using the 1.5 × IQR rule.




The IQR method confirms the Z-score findings for fraud_amount, transaction_amount, and loan_amount, and additionally highlights age and personal_income as having notable outliers. These will be important when interpreting segmentation results.

title: Fraud Detection: A Statistical Exploration of Consumer Transaction Data
text:
Correlation Analysis


Show the code
corr_vars = ['age', 'personal_income', 'family_income', 'credit_score',
             'loan_amount', 'transaction_amount', 'account_age_days',
             'num_prev_transactions', 'avg_transaction_value', 'fraud_amount']

corr = df_fraud[corr_vars].corr().round(2)

fig = go.Figure(data=go.Heatmap(
    z=corr.values,
    x=corr.columns, y=corr.columns,
    text=corr.values,
    texttemplate='%{text}',
    textfont={"size": 10, "family": "Inter, sans-serif"},
    colorscale='RdBu_r', zmin=-1, zmax=1,
    showscale=True, colorbar=dict(title='Correlation')
))
fig.update_layout(
    title='Correlation Matrix — Fraud Cases Only',
    height=600, width=700,
    font_family='Inter, sans-serif',
    yaxis=dict(autorange='reversed')
)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 3: Correlation matrix for quantitative features (fraud cases only).




Most variables show weak correlations with fraud_amount. The clearest exceptions are transaction_amount (r = 0.96), family_income, and personal_income. The strong relationship between transaction amount and fraud amount is expected — larger transactions can produce larger losses — but the correlation is not 1:1, because some frauds are partial (not the entire transaction is lost).

title: Fraud Detection: A Statistical Exploration of Consumer Transaction Data
text:
Exploratory Segmentation
Where the dataset gives its clearest signal is in the demographic breakdown of fraud cases. This is the part of the analysis I find most actionable from a business perspective.

Fraud amount by age group


Show the code
age_order = ['18–26', '26–34', '34–42', '42–50', '50–58', '58–66', '66–74', '74–82', '82–90']
fraud_by_age = df_fraud.groupby('Age Group', observed=True)['fraud_amount'].sum().reindex(age_order).fillna(0).reset_index()

fig = px.bar(
    fraud_by_age,
    x='Age Group', y='fraud_amount',
    title='Total Fraud Amount by Age Group',
    color='fraud_amount',
    color_continuous_scale='Blues',
    labels={'fraud_amount': 'Total Fraud Amount ($)'},
    template='plotly_white',
    text=fraud_by_age['fraud_amount'].apply(lambda x: f'${x:,.0f}')
)
fig.update_traces(textposition='outside')
fig.update_layout(height=450, font_family='Inter, sans-serif', showlegend=False)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 4: Total fraud amount by age group. The 34–42 group accounts for the highest monetary losses.




Customers aged 34 to 42 account for the highest monetary losses (~$71,700 in total), closely followed by the 42–50 group. This is the most commercially relevant finding — mid-career customers tend to have access to higher-value accounts and therefore represent larger losses per incident.


Fraud frequency by age group


Show the code
fraud_count_age = df_fraud['Age Group'].value_counts().reindex(age_order).fillna(0).reset_index()
fraud_count_age.columns = ['Age Group', 'Count']

fig = px.bar(
    fraud_count_age,
    x='Age Group', y='Count',
    title='Fraud Frequency by Age Group',
    color='Count',
    color_continuous_scale='Blues',
    template='plotly_white',
    text='Count'
)
fig.update_traces(textposition='outside')
fig.update_layout(height=450, font_family='Inter, sans-serif', showlegend=False)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 5: Number of fraud incidents per age group.




Counting cases rather than amounts gives a different picture: the 50–58 group has the highest number of incidents (54), but each one is typically smaller in value. In other words, the two age bands display different patterns:

34–42: fewer incidents, larger losses per case
50–58: more incidents, smaller losses per case

Both patterns matter for prevention strategy, but they call for different interventions.


Fraud by gender


Show the code
gender_age = df_fraud.groupby(['Age Group', 'gender'], observed=True).size().reset_index(name='Count')
gender_age['Age Group'] = pd.Categorical(gender_age['Age Group'], categories=age_order, ordered=True)
gender_age = gender_age.sort_values('Age Group')

fig = px.bar(
    gender_age,
    x='Age Group', y='Count', color='gender',
    barmode='group',
    title='Fraud Cases by Age Group and Gender',
    color_discrete_map={'Female': '#2f5dcc', 'Male': '#93c5fd'},
    template='plotly_white'
)
fig.update_layout(height=450, font_family='Inter, sans-serif')
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 6: Fraud cases by age group and gender.




Female customers are more frequently affected by fraud across nearly every age band, with the peak occurring in the 50–58 group (29 cases). This pattern is consistent with research on targeted scam techniques, though I would want a larger dataset before making strong causal claims.


Fraud by education level


Show the code
edu_age = df_fraud.groupby(['Age Group', 'education'], observed=True).size().reset_index(name='Count')
edu_age['Age Group'] = pd.Categorical(edu_age['Age Group'], categories=age_order, ordered=True)
edu_age = edu_age.sort_values('Age Group')

fig = px.bar(
    edu_age,
    x='Age Group', y='Count', color='education',
    barmode='group',
    title='Fraud Cases by Age Group and Education',
    color_discrete_sequence=['#1e3d99', '#2f5dcc', '#6a94f0', '#9db7f4', '#c9d9ff'],
    template='plotly_white'
)
fig.update_layout(height=480, font_family='Inter, sans-serif')
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 7: Fraud cases by education level and age group.




Master’s degree holders show the highest fraud frequency in the 34–42 band (27 cases), while High School is the dominant education level among older victims (17 cases in the 50–58 group). This may reflect different lifestyles and digital-engagement patterns — higher-educated, mid-career professionals are highly digital, which exposes them to different fraud vectors.


Fraud percentage by transaction type


Show the code
totals_type = df_fraud.groupby('transaction_type')[['transaction_amount', 'fraud_amount']].sum()
totals_type['Fraud_Pct'] = (totals_type['fraud_amount'] / totals_type['transaction_amount']) * 100
totals_type = totals_type.sort_values('Fraud_Pct', ascending=True).reset_index()

fig = px.bar(
    totals_type,
    x='Fraud_Pct', y='transaction_type',
    orientation='h',
    title='Fraud % of Total Transaction Amount — by Transaction Type',
    color='Fraud_Pct',
    color_continuous_scale='Blues',
    labels={'Fraud_Pct': 'Fraud %', 'transaction_type': 'Transaction type'},
    template='plotly_white',
    text=totals_type['Fraud_Pct'].apply(lambda x: f'{x:.1f}%')
)
fig.update_traces(textposition='outside')
fig.update_layout(height=380, font_family='Inter, sans-serif', showlegend=False)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 8: Fraud amount as a percentage of total transaction amount, per transaction type.




ATM transactions show the highest proportion of monetary loss relative to transaction volume (81%), followed by Online transactions (77%). This is operationally useful — it points to where monitoring and controls might have the highest marginal impact.

title: Fraud Detection: A Statistical Exploration of Consumer Transaction Data
text:
Predictive Modelling
After the exploratory analysis, I trained two classification models: a Decision Tree and a Random Forest. The goal was to see whether the demographic and behavioural features in this dataset could, on their own, predict whether a transaction is fraudulent.






ImportantA note on the modelling results



I want to be transparent: the models I trained delivered modest performance (accuracy around 57–58%). Rather than dismiss this, I treat it as a legitimate finding — the dataset, while clean and balanced, is only 500 rows, and the features available (demographics and transaction metadata) do not carry enough signal to achieve strong classification on their own. The analysis below shows what the models can tell us, and where they fall short.



Train / Test split


Show the code
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score,
                             f1_score, confusion_matrix)

y = df['is_fraud']
X = df.drop(columns=['is_fraud', 'transaction_amount', 'fraud_amount',
                     'customer_id', 'gender', 'education', 'marital_status',
                     'Age Group', 'transaction_type', 'device_type'])

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42
)

print(f"Train set: {len(X_train)} rows")
print(f"Test set:  {len(X_test)} rows")
print(f"\nTrain class balance:")
print(y_train.value_counts(normalize=True).round(3))

I dropped transaction_amount and fraud_amount from the feature set to avoid target leakage — these columns directly encode the fraud outcome and would inflate accuracy artificially.


Model comparison


Show the code
dt = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=11, random_state=42)

In a real banking setting, missing fraud is far more costly than over-flagging, so this model in its current form would not be appropriate for deployment.

This gives us a consistent story across three different analytical methods, which is more valuable than the raw accuracy number.

title: Fraud Detection: A Statistical Exploration of Consumer Transaction Data
text:
Key Findings






TipFinding 01 — Age-based fraud patterns are bimodal



The 34–42 age group has fewer fraud incidents but higher losses per case, while the 50–58 group has more incidents but smaller average loss. These represent two distinct fraud profiles that warrant different prevention strategies.








TipFinding 02 — Female customers are affected more frequently



Across nearly every age band, female customers represent a larger share of fraud cases. The pattern is robust in the data, though causation is beyond what this dataset can establish.








TipFinding 03 — ATM and Online channels carry the highest relative loss



ATM transactions showed fraud amounts equal to 81% of their total transaction volume, and Online close behind at 77%. These are the channels where monitoring investment is likely to have the highest return.








TipFinding 04 — Income is the most predictive signal



Across correlation analysis and Random Forest feature importance, income variables (personal and family) consistently emerge as the strongest predictors. Credit score is a close second.

title: Fraud Detection: A Statistical Exploration of Consumer Transaction Data
text:
Limitations and Reflection






WarningWhat this project cannot tell us



Dataset size. With only 500 rows, any model is operating in a low-data regime. Classification accuracy around 57% is a direct reflection of this: there simply isn’t enough signal in the available features to separate classes more cleanly. A production system would need tens or hundreds of thousands of transactions to train on.
Feature coverage. The dataset lacks features that are typically the most predictive in real fraud detection: transaction timestamps, merchant categories, geolocation, device fingerprints, and historical behavioural patterns. The demographic features available here are useful for segmentation, but insufficient for accurate prediction.
Causation vs correlation. The gender, age, and education patterns observed are correlations within this sample, not causal claims. Interpreting them as “female customers are more at risk” without additional evidence would be premature.
Model selection. I focused on Decision Tree and Random Forest because they handle mixed-type data well and are interpretable. Gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM) would likely improve the numerical results, but the fundamental constraints of dataset size and feature coverage would remain.

title: Fraud Detection: A Statistical Exploration of Consumer Transaction Data
text:
Recommendations
Based on the findings, and explicitly acknowledging the limitations above, I would recommend:

Focus fraud-prevention outreach on the 34–42 and 50–58 age groups — these concentrate the highest monetary losses and highest incident counts respectively.
Prioritise monitoring investment in ATM and Online channels where the fraud-to-transaction ratio is highest.
Extend the dataset before re-training models — adding transaction timestamps, merchant categories, and behavioural history would substantially improve classification performance.
Use this dataset for descriptive insight, not predictive deployment. The EDA findings are actionable; the models are not.

title: Fraud Detection: A Statistical Exploration of Consumer Transaction Data
text:
Conclusion
This project was an exercise in applying the full range of statistical techniques learned throughout the module — from descriptive statistics and outlier detection, through correlation analysis and segmentation, to classification modelling. The most valuable lesson I take from it is that a modest model result is still a meaningful outcome when interpreted honestly. The EDA findings are genuinely useful for a business stakeholder; the model is not production-ready, and saying so is more professional than claiming otherwise.
Being rigorous about what the data can and cannot support is, I think, the core skill of a Business Analyst — and this project gave me a clear opportunity to practise it.

What I set out to do
The project required developing a professional e-portfolio using Quarto, managing it with Git, and publishing it through GitHub Pages. While the initial brief seemed straightforward, the implementation revealed a significant gap between theoretical knowledge and practical competence. Integrating visual design with technical structure forced me to understand the workflow as a whole rather than as isolated steps, and this process helped me develop a more professional approach to building and presenting technical work.

title: Reflection
text:
Key skills developed
Quarto as a publishing framework. I came into this project expecting Quarto to be just for writing text, but I learned it is a much more powerful tool. It allowed me to separate the content (what I write) from the design (how it looks). Because of this, I could change the appearance of my entire site by editing just one file, which is much more efficient.
Reproducible analysis with Python. Integrating executable Python code directly into my portfolio pages was challenging, but the outcome was worth the effort. In previous courses, I exported Jupyter charts as images and pasted them into reports. Now, the charts are generated directly by the code, making the analysis fully reproducible and resulting in higher-quality visuals.

title: Reflection
text:
Challenges and technical learning
Certain obstacles during the project turned into some of the most valuable learning moments.






WarningThree technical challenges worth highlighting



1. YAML configuration. Changing the site theme required modifying the configuration file. What seemed like a simple edit resulted in some errors and delays. Understanding the strict enforcement of whitespace in YAML reinforced the importance of paying close attention to configuration syntax.
2. File permissions on deployment. My profile image initially failed to display on the live site despite being correctly referenced. The issue was related to file permissions inherited from macOS, which restricted public access. Applying the correct permissions resolved the issue and introduced me to a dimension of web publishing I had not previously considered.
3. Build cache. Sometimes, changes were not reflected because the program was serving an ‘old copy’ from its cache. I learned that troubleshooting requires more than just reviewing my code; it also involves clearing temporary files created by the system.


These three issues — YAML syntax, file permissions, and caching — They represent the type of operational knowledge that is covered in introductory courses, but it is in professional practice where we really learned.

title: Reflection
text:
What I would refine
Looking back, there are aspects of my workflow I would approach differently in future projects. I would deploy earlier, so that deployment issues could be isolated before too many changes accumulated. I would also adopt smaller, more frequent commits from the start, and maintain a concise working log throughout development to support a more detailed final reflection.

title: Financial News Sentiment Analysis: BERT vs FinBERT vs LLaMA 3.2
text:
Financial firms process thousands of news items daily to inform trading, risk, and portfolio decisions. Manually classifying sentiment at scale is infeasible. I benchmarked three NLP architectures on sentence-level sentiment classification to identify the most effective, production-ready solution for this domain.






NoteThe question



Which architecture delivers the best sentiment classification on financial text: general-purpose BERT, domain-pretrained FinBERT, or a much larger zero-shot LLaMA 3.2?

title: Financial News Sentiment Analysis: BERT vs FinBERT vs LLaMA 3.2
text:
Financial firms process thousands of news items daily to inform trading, risk, and portfolio decisions. Manually classifying sentiment at scale is infeasible. I benchmarked three NLP architectures on sentence-level sentiment classification to identify the most effective, production-ready solution for this domain.






NoteThe question



Which architecture delivers the best sentiment classification on financial text: general-purpose BERT, domain-pretrained FinBERT, or a much larger zero-shot LLaMA 3.2?

title: Financial News Sentiment Analysis: BERT vs FinBERT vs LLaMA 3.2
text:
The Approach
Dataset. Financial PhraseBank1 — 2,264 sentences from English-language financial news, each labelled by 16 finance experts with full agreement. Stratified 80/20 split to preserve class proportions.
Three models tested. BERT-base and FinBERT fine-tuned under identical hyperparameters (3 epochs, batch 16, AdamW optimiser at learning rate 2e-5). LLaMA 3.2 (3B parameters) run zero-shot via Ollama at temperature 0 — no fine-tuning.
Evaluation metrics. Accuracy, precision, recall, weighted F1, and confusion matrices. The last is critical for imbalanced data, where negative signals carry the highest business cost.

title: Financial News Sentiment Analysis: BERT vs FinBERT vs LLaMA 3.2
text:
Data Preparation
The cleaning step is intentionally minimal — transformer tokenisers handle most normalisation internally, so heavy preprocessing can actually hurt performance.


Show the code
import re
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

def clean_text(text):
    # Collapse whitespace only — let the tokeniser do the rest
    text = re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', str(text))
    return text.strip()

df['text']      = df['sentence'].apply(clean_text)
df['label_num'] = df['label'].map({'negative': 0, 'neutral': 1, 'positive': 2})

# Stratified 80/20 split preserves class proportions
train_texts, test_texts, train_labels, test_labels = train_test_split(
    df['text'].values,
    df['label_num'].values,
    test_size=0.2,
    random_state=42,
    stratify=df['label_num'].values
)

print(f"Train: {len(train_texts):,}  Test: {len(test_texts):,}")
# → Train: 1,811  Test: 453

title: Financial News Sentiment Analysis: BERT vs FinBERT vs LLaMA 3.2
text:
Model 1 — BERT (General-Purpose Baseline)
BERT-base-uncased was fine-tuned as a baseline to establish how a general-purpose model performs on financial text.


Show the code
from transformers import BertTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification, AdamW
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader
import torch

MAX_LEN    = 128
BATCH_SIZE = 16
EPOCHS     = 3
LR         = 2e-5

tokenizer = BertTokenizer.from_pretrained('bert-base-uncased')
model     = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    'bert-base-uncased',
    num_labels=3
)

optimiser = AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=LR)

# Training loop (abridged)
for epoch in range(EPOCHS):
    model.train()
    epoch_loss = 0
    for batch in train_loader:
        optimiser.zero_grad()
        outputs = model(**batch)
        outputs.loss.backward()
        optimiser.step()
        epoch_loss += outputs.loss.item()
    print(f"Epoch {epoch + 1}: avg loss = {epoch_loss / len(train_loader):.4f}")

text:
Model 2 — FinBERT (Domain-Pretrained)
FinBERT2 is BERT pre-trained on a large corpus of Reuters financial news before fine-tuning. The architecture and parameter count are identical to BERT-base (110M). The only difference is what the model has already been exposed to.


Show the code
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('yiyanghkust/finbert-tone')
model     = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    'yiyanghkust/finbert-tone',
    num_labels=3
)

# Fine-tuned with the same hyperparameters as BERT above
# (3 epochs, batch 16, AdamW, lr=2e-5)

title: Financial News Sentiment Analysis: BERT vs FinBERT vs LLaMA 3.2
text:
Model 3 — LLaMA 3.2 Zero-Shot
LLaMA 3.2 (3B) was tested in a fundamentally different paradigm: no training, no labelled examples. The model was prompted directly via Ollama to classify each sentence.


Show the code
import requests

PROMPT_TEMPLATE = """Classify the sentiment of this financial news sentence as exactly one of:
negative, neutral, or positive.

Sentence: "{sentence}"

Sentiment:"""

def llama_classify(sentence):
    response = requests.post('http://localhost:11434/api/generate', json={
        'model': 'llama3.2:3b',
        'prompt': PROMPT_TEMPLATE.format(sentence=sentence),
        'temperature': 0,
        'stream': False
    })
    return response.json()['response'].strip().lower()

# Run on all 453 test sentences
llama_predictions = [llama_classify(s) for s in test_texts]

text:
Results

Head-to-head comparison


Show the code
results = pd.DataFrame({
    'Model':     ['BERT (base)', 'FinBERT ★', 'LLaMA 3.2 (zero-shot)'],
    'Accuracy':  [0.821, 0.883, 0.868],
    'Precision': [0.823, 0.885, 0.870],
    'Recall':    [0.821, 0.883, 0.868],
    'F1':        [0.820, 0.884, 0.867]
})

results_long = results.melt(
    id_vars='Model',
    var_name='Metric',
    value_name='Score'
)

fig = px.bar(
    results_long,
    x='Model',
    y='Score',
    color='Metric',
    barmode='group',
    title='Weighted Metrics — BERT vs FinBERT vs LLaMA 3.2',
    color_discrete_sequence=['#1e3d99', '#2f5dcc', '#6a94f0', '#b9d0ff'],
    template='plotly_white',
    text=results_long['Score'].apply(lambda x: f'{x:.3f}')
)
fig.update_traces(textposition='outside', textfont_size=10)
fig.update_layout(
    height=500,
    yaxis=dict(range=[0.7, 0.95], title='Score (weighted)'),
    font_family='Inter, sans-serif',
    legend=dict(orientation='h', yanchor='bottom', y=-0.25, xanchor='center', x=0.5)
)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 4: All four weighted metrics across the three models. FinBERT leads; zero-shot LLaMA 3.2 is impressively close.










ImportantHeadline numbers




BERT fine-tuned: 82.1% accuracy — the general-purpose baseline
FinBERT fine-tuned: 88.3% accuracy — domain pre-training wins
LLaMA 3.2 zero-shot: 86.8% accuracy — no labels required





FinBERT confusion matrix
The confusion matrix for the winning model tells us more than the headline accuracy does — particularly where the errors concentrate.


Show the code
cm = np.array([
    [52, 7, 2],
    [14, 251, 13],
    [3, 14, 97]
])

labels = ['Negative', 'Neutral', 'Positive']

fig = go.Figure(data=go.Heatmap(
    z=cm,
    x=labels,
    y=labels,
    text=cm,
    texttemplate='%{text}',
    textfont={"size": 18, "family": "Inter, sans-serif"},
    colorscale=[[0, '#eef4ff'], [0.5, '#6a94f0'], [1, '#1e3d99']],
    showscale=True,
    colorbar=dict(title='Count')
))
fig.update_layout(
    title='FinBERT — Confusion Matrix (Test Set, n=453)',
    xaxis_title='Predicted',
    yaxis_title='Actual',
    height=500,
    width=600,
    font_family='Inter, sans-serif',
    yaxis=dict(autorange='reversed')
)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 5: FinBERT confusion matrix on the 453-sentence test set. Strong diagonal; most confusion is between neutral and the sentiment-bearing classes.




The diagonal is strong — FinBERT got most predictions right. The most interesting errors:

14 neutrals classified as negative (false alarms on negative sentiment)
14 positives classified as neutral (missed positive signals)

Most confusion lies on the neutral ↔︎ sentiment-bearing border, not between negative and positive. That makes intuitive sense: distinguishing “the company grew” from “the company did not shrink” is genuinely hard.


Per-class performance


Show the code
per_class = pd.DataFrame({
    'Class':       ['Negative', 'Neutral', 'Positive'] * 3,
    'F1':          [0.72, 0.86, 0.81,    # BERT
                    0.78, 0.91, 0.88,    # FinBERT
                    0.76, 0.90, 0.85],   # LLaMA
    'Model':       ['BERT'] * 3 + ['FinBERT'] * 3 + ['LLaMA 3.2'] * 3
})

fig = px.bar(
    per_class,
    x='Class',
    y='F1',
    color='Model',
    barmode='group',
    title='Per-Class F1 Score — All Three Models',
    color_discrete_sequence=['#b9d0ff', '#2f5dcc', '#0e1830'],
    template='plotly_white',
    text=per_class['F1'].apply(lambda x: f'{x:.2f}')
)
fig.update_traces(textposition='outside')
fig.update_layout(
    height=450,
    yaxis=dict(range=[0.6, 1.0], title='F1 score'),
    font_family='Inter, sans-serif'
)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 6: Per-class F1 score for each model. Negative class is consistently the weakest, across all three models.




The negative class is the bottleneck across every model — unsurprising given it has only 303 training examples. For a trading desk, this matters disproportionately: a missed negative signal is far more expensive than a missed positive one.

title: Financial News Sentiment Analysis: BERT vs FinBERT vs LLaMA 3.2
text:
What I Found






TipFinding 01 — Domain pre-training beats raw scale



FinBERT (110M parameters, pre-trained on Reuters financial news) outperformed both general BERT and the much larger LLaMA 3.2 (3B parameters). For specialised language, targeted pre-training matters more than model size.








TipFinding 02 — Zero-shot is surprisingly viable



LLaMA 3.2 reached 86.8% with zero labelled examples. For a firm without the budget to annotate thousands of sentences, this is a legitimate option — despite slower CPU inference and the lack of confidence scores.








TipFinding 03 — The minority class is the bottleneck



All three models showed the highest error on the negative class (303 of 2,264 rows). Per-class analysis mattered more than headline accuracy — the business value lives in catching negative signals.








TipFinding 04 — Recommendation



Deploy FinBERT for real-time sentiment on trading desks. Keep LLaMA 3.2 as a zero-shot fallback for edge languages or new domains where fine-tuning data does not yet exist.

title: Financial News Sentiment Analysis: BERT vs FinBERT vs LLaMA 3.2
text:
Limitations & Next Steps

Class imbalance. Oversampling the negative class, or using class weights, would likely lift per-class F1 further.
Inference cost. FinBERT is fast on GPU but not free; for latency-sensitive applications, a distilled version would be worth testing.
Domain drift. Financial language evolves (new instruments, new terminology). Periodic re-training on recent data is essential for production deployment.
Multilingual extension. The PhraseBank is English-only. For a bilingual markets desk, testing FinBERT-multilingual or XLM-R would be the natural next step.
